content: Fungal infections of the toenails, known as onychomycosis, are a common condition that can damage the nail's structure and appearance. In severe cases, this condition can interfere with daily activities. Treatment options include oral and topical antifungal medications, but topical treatments often have low success rates due to the nail's physical properties. Oral antifungal treatments tend to have shorter treatment durations and higher cure rates. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of oral antifungal treatments for toenail onychomycosis. The review included 48 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 10,200 participants. Most participants had subungual fungal infections of the toenails, and the studies lasted between 4 months and 2 years. The quality of the studies varied, with one study assessed as having a low risk of bias in all domains, while 18 studies had a high risk of bias in at least one domain, most commonly due to lack of blinding. High-quality evidence demonstrated that terbinafine was significantly more effective than placebo in achieving both clinical cure (risk ratio [RR] 6.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.96 to 9.08) and mycological cure (RR 4.53, 95% CI 2.47 to 8.33). Adverse events associated with terbinafine included gastrointestinal symptoms, infections, and headaches, but the risk of these events was likely not significantly different from placebo (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.47, moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, high-quality evidence showed that azoles were more effective than placebo for achieving clinical cure (RR 22.18, 95% CI 12.63 to 38.95) and mycological cure (RR 5.86, 95% CI 3.23 to 10.62). Adverse events in the azole group, such as headaches, flu-like symptoms, and nausea, were slightly more common but likely not significantly different from placebo (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.12, moderate-quality evidence). When comparing terbinafine and azoles, moderate-quality evidence suggested that terbinafine was probably more effective in achieving clinical cure (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.95) and mycological cure (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.88). The risk of adverse events was likely similar between the two groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.17), and there may be no difference in recurrence rates (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.79, low-quality evidence). Common adverse events in both groups included headaches, viral infections, and nausea. Moderate-quality evidence indicated that azoles and griseofulvin likely had similar efficacy for achieving clinical cure (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.96) and mycological cure (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.51). However, griseofulvin was associated with a higher risk of adverse events (RR 2.41, 95% CI 1.56 to 3.73), including gastrointestinal disturbances and allergic reactions. In contrast, azole-treated participants commonly experienced nausea and vomiting. Very low-quality evidence made it uncertain whether there was any difference in recurrence rates between these two treatments. Low-quality evidence suggested that terbinafine may be more effective than griseofulvin in achieving clinical cure (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.72) and mycological cure (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90). Griseofulvin was associated with a higher risk of adverse events (RR 2.09, 95% CI 1.15 to 3.82), including headaches and gastrointestinal issues, while terbinafine-treated participants reported taste disturbances and nausea. No studies addressed recurrence rates or quality of life for this comparison. In conclusion, high-quality evidence supports the effectiveness of terbinafine and azoles compared to placebo for both clinical and mycological cure of onychomycosis. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that terbinafine may be more effective than azoles, with a similar risk of adverse events. Azoles and griseofulvin likely have similar efficacy, but griseofulvin is associated with more adverse events. Terbinafine may be more effective and better tolerated than griseofulvin, though the evidence is of low quality. Only a few studies assessed recurrence rates, and the severity of adverse events was not consistently reported. The quality of evidence varied widely, with limitations in study design, such as unclear randomization and lack of blinding, being common reasons for downgrading the evidence.
